sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
Every January, in villages of the Godavari delta, men in pressed white shirts crowd around a ring of packed earth and watch two roosters fight with small blades tied to their legs. The fights have been illegal since 2014. They happen anyway, at hundreds of sites, with politicians in the front row.

Far to the south, on a hill above Tirupati, a temple kitchen makes laddus whose name is protected by law. In 2024 they became a national fight over ghee.

Andhra Pradesh is often like this: ancient habit and new money in the same frame. Its borders were drawn in 1953, enlarged in 1956 and cut in 2014. Its capital was written into law only in April 2026. It farms most of the shrimp India sells to the world. Today you meet it through what you can see: a dance on a brass plate, cloth painted with a bamboo pen, a sour leaf, a bull that bows.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Andhra Pradesh lies on India's south-east coast, facing the Bay of Bengal. Its neighbours are Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Inside its Godavari delta sits Yanam, a speck of Puducherry left over from French rule.

It has two historic regions. **Coastal Andhra** is the long strip of deltas, lagoons and ports from Srikakulam to Nellore; its three northern districts are called **Uttarandhra**. **Rayalaseema**, 'land of the Rayas', is the dry interior to the south-west. The capital is **Amaravati**, being built on the Krishna. The largest city is **Visakhapatnam**. There are **28 districts** since 31 December 2025.

One warning before any number: today's state is what remained after Telangana left on 2 June 2014. Figures from before 2014 usually describe the larger state with Hyderabad in it.

sections.title: The land
sections.intro_md:
Three things shape the state: a broken line of hills, two great rivers and a long, exposed coast.

The **Eastern Ghats** are not one wall but separate ranges, rising to Arma Konda (1,680 m) in the north, where Adivasi villages grow coffee. The **Godavari** and **Krishna** cross the whole Deccan and end here in two deltas that almost touch near Kolleru Lake. They became the rice bowl in the 1850s, when Arthur Cotton built weirs at Dowleswaram and Vijayawada; delta farmers still garland his statues. Behind the hills, **Rayalaseema** sits in a rain shadow: red soil, groundnut, millet, and the Penna cutting its gorge at Gandikota.

The **coast** was re-measured in 2025 at 1,053 km, third among states, and is hit by Bay of Bengal cyclones most years. The spotlights below run from the hills to the lagoons.

pins.label: Pulicat Lake, flamingos and the rocket island

spotlights.name: Papikondalu, the Godavari gorge
spotlights.when: Gorge cut through the Eastern Ghats
spotlights.spot_it: A wide brown river squeezed between steep green hills, with tourist launches in the middle.
spotlights.story_md: Below Bhadrachalam the Godavari, otherwise a broad plains river, forces its way through the Eastern Ghats. For about 60 km the hills close in and the river narrows and deepens. Locals call the hills Papikondalu. Boat trips run up the gorge from near Rajahmundry and Polavaram, past Koya and Konda Reddi villages that are reached mostly by water. The hills form Papikonda National Park, about 1,013 square kilometres. The view has a deadline: the Polavaram reservoir will raise the water level and drown part of the gorge and the villages along it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's most dramatic river landscape, and the one Polavaram will change most.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Godavari squeezes through the hills, and a dam downstream is about to fill the squeeze.

spotlights.name: Araku Valley and the Dhimsa

where.label: Alluri Sitarama Raju district, Eastern Ghats

spotlights.spot_it: Rolling green hills, shade-grown coffee, and lines of Adivasi women dancing with linked arms.
spotlights.story_md: Araku is a hill valley about 111 km from Visakhapatnam, at roughly 900 to 1,000 metres, reached by a slow train through dozens of tunnels. It is Adivasi country: Koya, Konda Dora, Bagata, Porja and others. Their signature dance is the **Dhimsa**: women link arms at the waist or shoulder and move in lines and circles to drums and a reed pipe, stepping in small, swaying patterns. The same dance is shared with Koraput across the Odisha border. Coffee came to these hills in the 19th century; Adivasi farmers now grow Arabica under shade trees, sold abroad as Araku coffee.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows the Andhra that is neither delta nor Deccan: forest, hills and Adivasi life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Linked arms, a swaying line, coffee under the trees: that is Araku.

spotlights.name: Gandikota gorge
spotlights.when: Fort from the 12th century on; gorge far older
spotlights.spot_it: A red sandstone canyon with a green river at the bottom and fort walls along the rim.
spotlights.story_md: The Penna river has cut a narrow gorge through red sandstone here, and a fort was built on the rim. A local chief under the Kalyani Chalukyas began it as a sand fort; the Pemmasani Nayakas made it a stronghold; the Golconda sultans took it in the 17th century and added a mosque and granary inside the walls. The name means roughly 'gorge fort'. Tourism boards sell it as India's Grand Canyon. It is smaller than that, and much quieter: you can sit on the rim at sunset with almost no one around.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best single picture of Rayalaseema's dry, rocky interior.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gandi means gorge: a fort on the lip of a red canyon.

spotlights.name: Belum Caves
spotlights.spot_it: Long lit tunnels of pale limestone, with stalactites like dripping wax.
spotlights.story_md: Belum is a limestone cave system of about 3.2 km, the second-longest known in the Indian subcontinent after Krem Liat Prah in Meghalaya. An old river, linked to the Chitravathi, dissolved the rock long ago. Villagers knew the caves for centuries; the British geologist Robert Bruce Foote recorded them in 1884, and a German team led by Herbert Daniel Gebauer mapped them in the early 1980s. Buddhist and Jain monks once used them, and pottery found inside goes back to about 4500 BCE. About 1.5 km is open to visitors, lit and with walkways.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that the dry interior once had rivers strong enough to hollow out hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Belum: 3.2 km of tunnels under a dry field, second only to Meghalaya.

spotlights.name: Borra Caves
spotlights.when: Limestone formed over millions of years
spotlights.spot_it: A huge cave mouth in the forest, and inside, lit columns of stalagmites.
spotlights.story_md: Borra means 'hole' in Telugu. The caves sit in the Ananthagiri hills on the way to Araku, with the Gosthani river running through part of the system. Dripping water has built stalactites and stalagmites that guides name after gods and animals; a rounded formation inside is worshipped as a Shiva lingam, and villagers tell a story of a cow falling through the roof. The railway to Araku passes right by, with a station named Borra Guhalu, so many visitors combine the train, the caves and the valley in one day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Pairs with Belum: one cave system in the north-east hills, one in the south-west plains.
spotlights.memory_hook: Borra = hole. A hole in the hill with its own railway station.

spotlights.name: Kolleru Lake and its pelicans

where.label: Between the Godavari and Krishna deltas, near Eluru

spotlights.spot_it: A flat, shallow lake with half-drowned trees full of nesting pelicans and storks.
spotlights.story_md: Kolleru is one of India's largest freshwater lakes, filling the low ground between the two great deltas. In winter it hosts migrating birds, and its most famous residents are spot-billed pelicans, which nest in colonies at places such as Atapaka. It has been a Ramsar wetland since 2002, with a designated area of 90,100 hectares at full flood. The problem is visible from the air: much of the lake edge has been dug into fish and shrimp ponds. Courts have ordered ponds removed; many came back. Water, money and birds argue here every year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's environmental argument in one place.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pelicans in the middle, shrimp ponds at the edges.

spotlights.name: Pulicat Lake, flamingos and the rocket island

where.label: Tirupati district, on the Tamil Nadu border

spotlights.spot_it: Pink flamingos in a shallow lagoon, and on the sand bar beyond it, India's rocket launch pads.
spotlights.story_md: Pulicat is India's second-largest brackish lagoon after Chilika, about 759 square kilometres, most of it in Andhra Pradesh. In winter greater flamingos, painted storks and pelicans feed in its shallows, and the state holds a flamingo festival. The long barrier island that separates the lagoon from the Bay of Bengal is **Sriharikota**, home of ISRO's Satish Dhawan Space Centre. Every Indian satellite launch, including the Chandrayaan Moon missions, lifts off a few kilometres from flamingo water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One lagoon holds both a bird sanctuary and India's space port.
spotlights.memory_hook: Flamingos on one side of the sand bar, rockets on the other.

spotlights.name: Visakhapatnam's coast
spotlights.spot_it: A long curved beach road with green hills dropping straight to the sea.
spotlights.story_md: Vizag is the rare Indian city where hills meet the sea. The Eastern Ghats run right down to the Bay of Bengal, so the beach road curves between headlands, and from Kailasagiri hill you see the whole bay. RK Beach is the city's promenade, with a decommissioned submarine, INS Kursura, parked on the sand as a museum. Behind the beach is serious industry: a major port, the Navy's Eastern Command, the steel plant and the Hindustan Shipyard. The road north runs to Bheemili, an old Dutch trading town.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's largest city and its face to the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hills, sea and a submarine parked on the sand.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
Census 2011 counted **49,577,103** people inside today's borders, about 4.1% of India; projections put 2026 near **5.37 crore**. The 2027 census will replace these numbers.

Density was 304 people per square kilometre, below India's 382. Seven in ten lived in villages. The sex ratio was **997 women per 1,000 men**, close to parity. Literacy was **67.35%**, below the national 73%. Telugu is the mother tongue of 89%, Urdu of 6.6%. Hindus are 90.9%, Muslims 7.3%, Christians 1.4%.

Poverty fell fast before the pandemic: NITI Aayog's multidimensional index, which counts deprivation in health, schooling and living standards, rated **6.06%** of people poor in 2019-21, against 14.96% for India.

sections.title: Deep history
sections.intro_md: Ashoka's edicts at Erragudi show the Mauryan empire reached here by the 3rd century BCE, and Buddhism came with it. The **Satavahanas** (about 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE) ruled the Deccan partly from Dhanyakataka, beside Amaravati, and enlarged its great stupa. The **Ikshvakus** followed at Nagarjunakonda. The **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** (from 624) made Telugu a written literature: around **1022** the poet Nannaya began the Telugu Mahabharata at Rajahmundry. The **Kakatiyas** of Warangal united the Telugu lands; Marco Polo praised their queen **Rudramadevi** around 1290. **Vijayanagara** held the south until 1565; Krishnadevaraya wrote Telugu poetry and Lepakshi was painted under his successor. Then the **Qutb Shahis** of Golconda, whose port Machilipatnam shipped Kalamkari to Persia; the Mughals and the **Nizams**; and from 1766 and 1800 the British, who ruled the coast and Rayalaseema from Madras while Telangana stayed with the Nizam.

spotlights.name: Amaravati stupa and its sculpture
spotlights.spot_it: Crowded, moving limestone figures in a pale green-white stone, every panel packed edge to edge.
spotlights.story_md: Beside the Satavahana capital of Dhanyakataka stood the Mahachaitya, a great stupa wrapped in carved limestone panels telling the Buddha's life. The **Amaravati school** carved bodies in motion, overlapping and twisting, and in early panels the Buddha is shown only by symbols: an empty throne, footprints, a tree. The style travelled to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. In the 19th century the mound was dug up and much of it burned for lime. What survived was shipped off: about 120 pieces are in the British Museum, others in Chennai and Paris. At the site today, only the brick base remains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great art style born in the Telugu country, and now scattered across three continents.
spotlights.memory_hook: The stupa is in London, Chennai and Paris. The hole is in Amaravati.

spotlights.name: Lepakshi temple

where.label: Sri Sathya Sai district, near Hindupur

spotlights.spot_it: A pillar that hangs above the floor, a giant stone bull, and painted ceilings in faded red and black.
spotlights.story_md: Two brothers who served the Vijayanagara king Achyuta Deva Raya built the Veerabhadra temple around 1530. Three things make it famous. One pillar of the dance hall does not quite touch the floor: guides slide a cloth or paper under it. The ceilings carry some of the best-preserved Vijayanagara paintings, including a Veerabhadra often called among the largest single-figure murals in India. And 200 metres away lies a Nandi carved from one granite boulder, usually given as about 8 metres long and 4.5 metres high. Local legend says the name comes from 'le pakshi', 'rise, bird', said by Rama to the dying Jatayu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best place to see Vijayanagara painting, not just Vijayanagara stone.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hanging pillar, a giant bull, and a bird told to rise.

sections.title: Freedom and the making of the state
sections.intro_md:
By 1900 Telugu speakers in the Madras Presidency felt outnumbered by Tamil speakers in jobs and colleges. In 1913 the Andhra Mahasabha at Bapatla asked for a separate province. In 1937 coast and Rayalaseema leaders signed the **Sri Bagh Pact**: the richer coast promised the interior water, a university and the capital or High Court of any future state. It is still quoted.

After independence Nehru delayed language states. Potti Sriramulu's fast forced his hand, and **Andhra State** was born on **1 October 1953**, capital Kurnool. On **1 November 1956** the Telugu districts of Hyderabad State joined it to form **Andhra Pradesh**, capital Hyderabad. Telangana resented the merger (1969), the coast answered with Jai Andhra (1972), and on **2 June 2014** Telangana became a separate state, taking Hyderabad with it.

spotlights.name: Alluri Sitarama Raju
spotlights.spot_it: Usually drawn in saffron with a bow and arrows, though his men fought with captured guns.
spotlights.story_md: In 1882 the Madras Forest Act closed the hill forests and banned podu, the shifting cultivation of the Adivasi hill people. Alluri Sitarama Raju, a young sannyasi from the plains, led their revolt. From August 1922 his fighters raided police stations in the Rampa hills for rifles and ammunition, and for almost two years the British could not catch him. He was captured in the Chintapalli forest and shot by police at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924, still in his twenties. A district created in 2022 and the new international airport at Bhogapuram carry his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The freedom struggle in the forests, led for and with Adivasi people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Raided police stations for guns; now an airport carries his name.

spotlights.name: Pingali Venkayya and the flag
spotlights.spot_it: The man in the relief handing Gandhi a striped flag; the flag behind India's tricolour.
spotlights.story_md: Pingali Venkayya, from Bhatlapenumarru near Machilipatnam, was a geologist, a linguist and an obsessive student of flags. At the Congress session in Vijayawada in 1921 he gave Gandhi a design in two colours: red for Hindus and green for Muslims. Gandhi asked for a white stripe for everyone else and a spinning wheel for self-reliance. That became the Swaraj flag, and the tricolour adopted on 22 July 1947 descends from it, with the wheel replaced by the Ashoka chakra. Venkayya died poor in 1963. A stamp came in 2009.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every Indian flag starts from a design shown to Gandhi in Vijayawada.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red, green, then Gandhi's white: the flag began in Vijayawada.

spotlights.name: Potti Sriramulu
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, bald man in a dhoti, on stamps and on statues in every Andhra town.
spotlights.story_md: Nehru did not want states drawn by language; he feared they would pull India apart. On 19 October 1952 Potti Sriramulu, a quiet Gandhian worker, began a fast unto death in Madras for a Telugu state. He died on the 58th day, 15 December 1952. Riots spread along the coast, and four days later Nehru announced that Andhra State would be formed. It came into being on 1 October 1953 with its capital at Kurnool, usually called the first state of independent India formed on the basis of language. People call him Amarajeevi, 'the immortal'. Nellore district carries his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His death forced India to redraw its map by language.
spotlights.memory_hook: 58 days without food, and India's map changed.

sections.title: Language and dialects
sections.intro_md:
**Telugu** is the mother tongue of 89% of the state and of about 83 million people in India (2011), the fourth most spoken native language in the country. It was declared a classical language on 8 August 2008. It is Dravidian, closer to Gondi and Kui than to Tamil, with a large Sanskrit vocabulary. Its literature starts with Nannaya around 1022.

Dialects follow the regions: coastal, Rayalaseema, North Andhra, and Telangana across the border. Print and film Telugu lean on the speech of the Krishna and Godavari deltas. Urdu is the second official language. In the hills, Adivasi languages such as Koya, Kuvi and Savara are spoken.

Politeness is grammar: *garu* after a name marks respect, *andi* softens almost anything. And Telugu travels: US speakers grew 86% between 2010 and 2017.

spotlights.name: The Telugu script
spotlights.when: From southern Brahmi; literary from c. 1022 CE
spotlights.spot_it: Round letters that look like loops and hooks, many with a tick on top: తెలుగు.
spotlights.story_md: Telugu letters are built from circles and curves, each consonant carrying a small check mark (the talakattu) on top. The script grew from the same southern Brahmi line as Kannada; the two parted in the Middle Ages and still look like cousins. A common explanation for the roundness is that scribes wrote on palm leaves with a metal stylus, and straight lines along the grain would split the leaf. Almost every native Telugu word ends in a vowel, which is why the 15th-century Venetian traveller Niccolò de' Conti is credited with calling it 'the Italian of the East'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: About 83 million people in India read and speak it, the fourth largest mother tongue in the country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Loops with ticks on top, every word ending in a vowel.

sections.title: Faith and philosophy
sections.intro_md:
For about six centuries the lower Krishna was one of Asia's great Buddhist regions, with monasteries at Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Bhattiprolu; in 2006 the Dalai Lama gave the Kalachakra initiation at Amaravati to over 100,000 people. Today most people are Hindu, and the map of faith is a map of hill temples: Tirumala in the south, Srisailam in the Nallamala forest, Srikalahasti, Simhachalam above Vizag, Kanaka Durga at Vijayawada. Under them runs a village religion of goddesses and fairs.

The state also produced its sceptics and seekers: Vemana's verses against hypocrisy, Potuluri Veerabrahmam's prophecies, Jiddu Krishnamurti from Madanapalle, who refused to be anyone's guru. Islam and Christianity have deep roots too: Nellore's Bara Shaheed Dargah holds the Rottela Panduga, a festival of exchanging flatbreads, and the coast has large Lutheran and Baptist communities.

spotlights.name: Tirumala Venkateswara temple
spotlights.when: Worship recorded from the early centuries CE; grew under Pallavas, Cholas, Vijayanagara
spotlights.spot_it: A gold-covered shrine tower, pilgrims with freshly shaved heads, and queues that last hours.
spotlights.story_md: On the seventh of seven hills above Tirupati stands the temple of Venkateswara, a form of Vishnu. It is one of the most visited and richest religious sites in the world. Many pilgrims climb the stone stairway from Alipiri at night. Many shave their heads as an offering; the temple sells the hair abroad for wigs. After hours in the queue comes a few seconds before the image. The temple trust, TTD, runs hospitals, colleges, its own TV channel and the kitchen that makes the laddu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The religious and economic centre of gravity of the south of the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shaved heads, a gold tower and a laddu at the end of the queue.

spotlights.name: Srikalahasti temple
spotlights.when: Shrine from at least the Chola period
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white gopuram by a river, and inside, a lamp said to flicker in still air.
spotlights.story_md: Srikalahasti worships Shiva as Vayu, the wind, one of the five element temples of south India. Its name joins three devotees from its legend: Sri the spider, Kala the snake and Hasti the elephant. The hunter Kannappa is said to have offered his own eyes here. Today the temple is busy with Rahu-Ketu rituals for people with an unlucky horoscope. In May 2010 its 500-year-old main gopuram cracked and collapsed; a new one was built and opened in 2017. The same town is the home of pen Kalamkari.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The wind temple, and the town where temple cloths are painted.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spider, snake, elephant: Sri-Kala-Hasti.

spotlights.name: Simhachalam temple
spotlights.spot_it: A grey stone temple on a forested hill above Vizag, its god hidden under sandalwood paste.
spotlights.story_md: On a hill at the edge of Visakhapatnam, Vishnu is worshipped as Varaha Narasimha, part boar, part lion. The present temple was built in the 13th century by the Eastern Ganga king Narasimha Deva I and consecrated in 1268, in the Kalinga style of Odisha, which is why it looks unlike temples further south. Its strangest custom: the image is covered in a thick layer of sandalwood paste all year, so it looks like a lump. Only on Akshaya Tritiya, in April or May, is the paste removed for a few hours, the Chandanotsavam.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A northern, Odisha-style temple on the Andhra coast.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god hidden in sandalwood, unveiled one day a year.

spotlights.name: Nagarjuna

where.label: Tied by tradition to the Krishna valley

spotlights.spot_it: Shown as a seated monk with a hood of snakes over his head.
spotlights.story_md: Nagarjuna is often called the most important Buddhist philosopher after the Buddha; Tibetans call him the second Buddha. He founded the **Madhyamaka**, the Middle Way school, which argues that nothing exists on its own: everything depends on parts, causes and the names we give it. Tradition links him to the Satavahana court and to Sriparvata in the Krishna valley, and Nagarjunakonda, the valley later flooded by the Nagarjuna Sagar dam, carries his name. Historians still argue over where he actually lived. His Root Verses on the Middle Way are studied from Japan to Tibet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Telugu-country thinker who shaped how half of Asia thinks.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nothing stands alone: the second Buddha of the Krishna valley.

spotlights.name: Annamacharya
spotlights.spot_it: A singer with hand cymbals, usually shown with a tambura or in prayer.
spotlights.story_md: Annamacharya, or Annamayya, from Tallapaka, is said to have written 32,000 songs (sankirtanas) to Venkateswara of Tirumala, in Telugu and Sanskrit. Between 12,000 and 14,000 survive because his family engraved them on copper plates between about 1525 and 1545. The plates lay forgotten in a vault at Tirumala until they were found in 1922. His songs, such as 'Brahmam okkate' ('there is only one Brahman', a song that says the king and the servant sleep on the same earth), are sung in concerts and temples every day. He is often called the first great composer of Telugu song.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great voice of Telugu devotional music, saved by copper.
spotlights.memory_hook: 32,000 songs, copper plates, a forgotten vault.

spotlights.name: Vemana
spotlights.spot_it: Four-line Telugu verses ending 'Vishwadabhirama vinura vema'.
spotlights.story_md: Vemana wrote short, blunt verses in plain Telugu that mock caste, empty ritual, greed and hypocrisy. Each ends with the same refrain, 'Vishwadabhirama vinura vema', 'listen, Vema'. One of the best known says, roughly: a drop of milk from a good cow is enough, a potful from a donkey is useless; a little from a good person beats a lot from a bad one. In the 1820s the British official C. P. Brown collected his verses and published translations, and Vemana is still quoted at dinner tables as proverbs. A university in Kadapa is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The voice of the sceptic in Telugu culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: One good cow's drop beats a donkey's potful.

spotlights.name: Ammavaru jatara: the village goddess fair

where.label: Every village; big ones at Vizianagaram and Tirupati

spotlights.spot_it: A priest swung through the sky on a long pole above a roaring crowd.
spotlights.story_md: Beyond the big temples, most Andhra villages are protected by a goddess, an ammavaru: Gangamma, Pydithalli, Poleramma, Maremma. Her yearly jatara (fair) brings processions, drums, goats and chickens, pots carried on heads, and the whole village home. The most dramatic is the **Sirimanu** festival of Pydithalli Ammavaru in Vizianagaram: a priest is fixed to the tip of a long wooden pole and swung over the crowd in a slow arc. At Tirupati, during the Gangamma jatara, men dress as women and wear disguises for a week.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows the Hinduism of the village, older and louder than the temple kind.
spotlights.memory_hook: A priest on a 50-foot pole, swinging over Vizianagaram.

sections.title: Dance, music, theatre
sections.intro_md:
Andhra's performing arts are mostly storytelling. The classical form, Kuchipudi, began as all-night dance-drama by village men. Burra katha is a ballad sung by three people. Tholu bommalata tells the epics with coloured shadows. Harikatha, a solo of song and story, fills temple courtyards. In the hills, Adivasi women dance the Dhimsa (see Araku).

Music sits under all of it. Telugu is the main language of Carnatic music, through Tyagaraja (born in Tamil Nadu), Annamacharya and Kshetrayya, whose love songs are danced in both Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam. The instrument the state calls its own is the Bobbili veena. Telugu cinema, now based in Hyderabad, is the art most people actually watch, and its stars move into politics.

Watch the clips: the difference between Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam is easier to see than to read.

spotlights.name: Kuchipudi
spotlights.spot_it: Quick, springy footwork, rounded movement, spoken lines, and the dancer balanced on the rim of a brass plate.
spotlights.story_md: One of India's eight classical dances is named after a single village in Krishna district. For centuries it belonged to troupes of Brahmin men who staged dance-dramas through the night and played the women's roles. Tradition credits Siddhendra Yogi with *Bhama Kalapam*, the story of Krishna's proud wife Satyabhama, still its signature piece. In the 20th century Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastri began teaching women and Vempati Chinna Satyam built the solo concert style. The showpiece is the **tarangam**: the dancer keeps time on the rim of a brass plate, sometimes with a pot of water on the head, to verses from Narayana Teertha's *Krishna Leela Tarangini*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Andhra's classical dance, and the one most people outside the state can name.
spotlights.memory_hook: If she is dancing on a plate, it is Kuchipudi.

compare.difference: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu) is geometric and angular, built on a deep half-sitting stance, and is danced silently. Kuchipudi is rounder and quicker, has acting and speech inside it, and ends with the brass-plate tarangam.

spotlights.name: Burra katha

where.label: Villages of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana

spotlights.spot_it: Three performers: a lead with a tambura and two side players with small drums who interrupt with jokes.
spotlights.story_md: Burra katha is a sung ballad with three people. The lead singer stands in the middle with a tambura (the gourd at its end is the burra) and tells a story in song and speech, stepping back and forth. Two side players beat small drums, answer him and crack jokes, one the comic, one the political commentator. Shows run for hours. In the 1940s the communist movement in the Telangana and Andhra countryside used it for propaganda, and governments in turn used it to spread health and literacy messages. Its best-known performer, Shaik Nazar, was a Muslim singer of Hindu epics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Theatre with no stage: the village news, history and politics, sung.
spotlights.memory_hook: One tambura, two drums, three voices, many hours.

spotlights.name: Tholu bommalata, leather shadow puppets

where.label: Nimmalakunta, Sri Sathya Sai district, and travelling troupes

spotlights.when: All-night shows; GI tag for Andhra leather puppetry
spotlights.spot_it: Tall, jointed puppets of translucent coloured leather, lit from behind so their colours glow on a screen.
spotlights.story_md: Tholu means leather; bommalata means doll play. Puppeteers cut figures from goat or deer hide, scrape them thin until light passes through, paint them in red, green and black, and punch tiny holes for detail. Many are as tall as a person, jointed at shoulders, elbows and knees. Behind a white screen lit by lamps, families of puppeteers perform the Ramayana and Mahabharata through the night, with songs and two comic characters, Ketigadu and Bangarakka. Unlike most shadow theatre, the audience sees coloured shadows. Nimmalakunta village is the best-known centre today, and many families now make lampshades and wall hangings as well.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ancestor-cousin of Indonesian wayang, still made by hand in one Andhra village.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leather so thin you see the colour through it.

spotlights.name: Bobbili veena
spotlights.spot_it: A full-size veena whose body, neck and dragon head are all carved from one block of jackfruit wood.
spotlights.story_md: Most veenas are joined from several pieces. The Bobbili veena is an ekanda veena, carved from a single block of seasoned jackfruit wood, so it has no joints that can loosen. The craft came up under the Bobbili rajas, and families in Gollapalli village near Bobbili still carve them by hand, with painted or inlaid decoration. Besides full concert instruments they make small decorative veenas, often given to visiting dignitaries as the state's official gift. The instrument got a GI tag in 2011.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the few instruments in India that is a protected regional product.
spotlights.memory_hook: One tree, one veena, no joints.

sections.title: Crafts and GI tags
sections.intro_md:
Andhra's crafts are about materials: natural dyes on cotton, soft tella poniki wood, lac melted by friction, jackfruit wood, translucent leather. Many hold a GI tag (geographical indication): Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam Kalamkari, Kondapalli and Etikoppaka toys, the Bobbili veena, leather puppetry, Budithi bell metal, Durgi stone carving, Udayagiri wooden cutlery and Narasapur crochet lace.

A GI tag means only producers from the named place can use the name. It does not mean the craft is thriving. Whether it raises carvers' and painters' incomes is a separate question, and for most of these crafts the honest answer is 'not yet enough'.

The test for today: can you tell pen Kalamkari from block Kalamkari, and Kondapalli wood from Etikoppaka lacquer, by sight?

spotlights.name: Kalamkari
spotlights.when: Trade cloth since at least the 17th century
spotlights.spot_it: Cloth painted in natural reds, black, ochre and indigo; pen style tells stories, block style repeats flowers and trees.
spotlights.story_md: Kalamkari joins the Persian words for pen (qalam) and craft. Only natural dyes are used, and one cloth may go through more than twenty rounds of washing, mordanting, dyeing and drying. There are two schools. In **Srikalahasti** artists draw freehand with a bamboo pen and fill the outlines by hand, making temple hangings that tell the Ramayana and Mahabharata in panels, often with Telugu captions. In **Machilipatnam** and nearby **Pedana**, outlines are printed with carved wooden blocks, and the motifs are flowering trees, vines and birds made for the Persian market, which Machilipatnam's port once served.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Andhra's best-known art, and a record of its old trade with Persia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pen tells a story; block repeats a garden.

compare.difference: Srikalahasti (pen): freehand outlines, gods and epic scenes in panels, often captioned. Machilipatnam (block): printed outlines, repeating flowers, trees of life and Persian-style medallions, no story.

spotlights.name: Kondapalli toys
spotlights.when: Craft families traced to the 16th century
spotlights.spot_it: Light, matte, brightly painted wooden figures: village couples, elephants with howdahs, the ten avatars.
spotlights.story_md: Kondapalli toys are carved from tella poniki, a soft, very light wood from the Kondapalli hills. Parts are carved separately and joined with makku, a paste of tamarind seed powder and sawdust, then coated with lime and painted in bright colours. The best-known sets show the ten avatars of Vishnu, village scenes such as a toddy tapper climbing a palm, and the Ambari elephant. The craft families trace their arrival from Rajasthan to the 16th century. Every Sankranti and Dasara, families arrange them on steps as part of the bommala koluvu, the doll display.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The toy that sits in almost every Telugu home's festival doll display.
spotlights.memory_hook: Feather-light wood, tamarind glue, ten avatars.

spotlights.name: Etikoppaka toys

where.label: Etikoppaka, on the Varaha river, Anakapalli district

spotlights.spot_it: Round, glossy, lacquered toys with no sharp corners, in deep red, yellow and green.
spotlights.story_md: Etikoppaka toys are turned on a lathe from ankudu wood (*Wrightia tinctoria*). While the wood spins, the turner presses a stick of lac mixed with natural plant colours against it. Friction heat melts the lac into a hard, shiny skin. No paint, no sharp edges, nothing to chip, which made them a favourite safe toy for small children. Spinning tops, rattles, bangle boxes and little figures come off the lathe in minutes. Village artisans revived natural dyes in the 1990s, and the toys were praised on national radio in 2020 as an example of Indian-made toys.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows a craft that solved child safety with friction and lac.
spotlights.memory_hook: No paint: the colour is melted on by spinning.

sections.title: Handloom
sections.intro_md:
Four handloom traditions of the state hold GI registration, and they map neatly onto its regions. On the coast, **Uppada** weaves feather-light silk jamdani and **Mangalagiri** crisp everyday cotton. In the south, **Venkatagiri** weaves some of the finest cotton in India. In Rayalaseema, **Dharmavaram** weaves heavy gold-bordered wedding silk.

Handloom is still one of the largest sources of work after farming, and one of the most fragile. Powerlooms copy the designs at a fraction of the price, and yarn prices swing. Commons, the open image library this app uses, has almost no good photos of Uppada or Venkatagiri sarees, so two of the spotlights below have no picture yet. Look them up before you buy one.

spotlights.name: Mangalagiri cotton
spotlights.spot_it: Crisp plain cotton with a woven gold zari border and no motifs on the body.
spotlights.story_md: Mangalagiri, a temple town between Vijayawada and Guntur, weaves cotton sarees and dress fabric on pit looms. The look is restrained: a plain or checked body, no printed or embroidered design, and a woven zari border, often the 'Nizam border' of small temple-like triangles. The fabric is combed cotton, tightly woven, so it stays crisp and is easy to wash. Weavers say the town's tradition goes back to the 15th century. It is everyday wear for teachers and office workers across the state, and it is GI-registered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's daily-wear cotton: plain body, gold edge.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plain middle, gold border, temple town.

spotlights.name: Venkatagiri sarees
spotlights.spot_it: Very fine, almost sheer cotton, often with small woven motifs and a zari border.
spotlights.story_md: Venkatagiri weavers are known for some of the finest cotton in south India: very high thread counts, light enough to feel like silk-cotton. The Velugoti rajas of Venkatagiri patronised the weavers from the 18th century, and the sarees were once made for the royal household. Motifs such as parrots, leaves and coins are woven in with the jamdani technique, an extra weft added by hand during weaving, and borders carry zari. The style is GI-registered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The finest cotton in the state, woven for a royal house.
spotlights.memory_hook: Venkatagiri: cotton so fine it floats.

spotlights.name: Uppada Jamdani
spotlights.spot_it: Feather-light silk with woven gold motifs that look embroidered but are part of the weave.
spotlights.story_md: Uppada is a fishing village on the coast north of Kakinada whose weavers make silk sarees in the jamdani technique, an extra-weft method from Bengal in which motifs are added thread by thread on the loom. The result is a saree so light it can be folded into a matchbox, so the boast goes, with gold or coloured motifs that sit inside the cloth rather than on top. A single saree can take two weavers weeks. The style is GI-registered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows the Bengali jamdani technique, adopted and made local on the Andhra coast.
spotlights.memory_hook: Uppada: a fishing village that weaves silk light as air.

spotlights.name: Dharmavaram silk
spotlights.spot_it: Heavy wedding silk with broad contrast borders, gold zari and temple motifs.
spotlights.story_md: Dharmavaram, a dry town in Rayalaseema, is one of the state's great silk centres. Its sarees use mulberry silk and gold zari, with wide borders in a contrasting colour and a heavy pallu often woven with temple, peacock or elephant designs. They are wedding silks: brides and their mothers buy them, and the weight of the zari is part of the point. Thousands of families in the town work at handlooms and, increasingly, powerlooms, and the weavers' debts and suicides in drought years have made the town a byword for the strain on handloom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Rayalaseema wedding silk, and a barometer of weavers' distress.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dharmavaram: heavy gold for a wedding, woven in a drought town.

sections.title: Food
sections.intro_md:
Andhra food is known for heat, and the heat is local: Guntur is the chilli capital. But the plate changes with the land.

In the **deltas**: rice, fish and prawns, gongura, pesarattu for breakfast, pulasa in the flood season, pulihora (tamarind rice) at temples. In **Rayalaseema**: ragi sangati, jonna rotte (sorghum flatbread), country chicken, and the most fiery cooking. In **Uttarandhra and the hills**: millets, forest produce, coffee.

A full meal, bhojanam, runs in a set order on a leaf or steel plate. Every family makes avakaya in summer. And every meal ends with curd rice, because after this much chilli you need it.

regions.name: Coastal
regions.note: rice, seafood, gongura, pootharekulu, Bandar laddu

regions.name: Rayalaseema
regions.note: ragi sangati, natukodi, jonna rotte, the hottest chilli use

spotlights.name: Andhra meals
spotlights.spot_it: Rice in the middle of a banana leaf ringed by pappu, koora, pickle, podi, ghee, pulusu and curd.
spotlights.story_md: A full Andhra meal, bhojanam, comes in a set order. First hot rice with ghee and a spoon of podi (spiced lentil powder) or pickle. Then **pappu**, lentils cooked with tomato, mango or greens. A dry vegetable **koora**. A sour **pulusu** or thin **charu** (rasam). Then curd rice to cool down, with a bite of pickle. Fried appadams and a sweet sit at the edge. Restaurants serve it 'unlimited': waiters keep coming with buckets until you fold the leaf. The heat comes from fresh and dried chilli in almost every dish.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The plate is the clearest way to meet the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice, ghee, podi, pappu, pulusu, curd: in that order.

spotlights.name: Gongura pachadi

where.label: Statewide; leaves sold fresh in Guntur

spotlights.spot_it: A dark green-black, very sour, very hot relish served with raw onion.
spotlights.story_md: Gongura are the leaves of the roselle plant, with red or green stems; the red ones are sourer. Cooked down with fried red chillies, garlic and salt into a thick pachadi (relish), they make the most Andhra-tasting thing on the plate: sharp, sour and fiery at once. It is eaten mixed into hot rice with ghee and a raw onion on the side. Gongura is so tied to the state that it is often half-jokingly called Andhra's mother, and jars of it travel in the luggage of every Telugu student going abroad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The taste most Telugus name first when they talk about home food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sour leaf, hot chilli, raw onion: gongura.

spotlights.name: Avakaya
spotlights.spot_it: Red, oily chunks of raw mango with the stone still in, from a ceramic jar.
spotlights.story_md: Avakaya is raw mango cut into pieces with its hard stone still attached, mixed with mustard powder (avalu, which gives the name), chilli powder, salt, and a lot of sesame or groundnut oil. Families make it once a year, in summer, when sour mango varieties arrive, cutting dozens of mangoes with a special knife and filling big ceramic jars (jaadi). The jar then lasts the year. Recipes are guarded and argued over like property, and the first spoon of the new season with hot rice and ghee is an event.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A once-a-year family ritual disguised as a pickle.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mustard, chilli, oil, and the mango stone left in.

spotlights.name: Pesarattu
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, green-flecked crepe, often with upma folded inside, served with ginger chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Pesarattu is a dosa made from whole green gram (pesalu) soaked and ground with ginger, green chilli and a little rice, with no fermentation and no urad dal. That makes it quick: soak overnight, grind in the morning, cook. It is spread thin on a hot griddle, sprinkled with chopped onion and cumin, and served with a sharp ginger chutney. In the Godavari districts and Vijayawada the classic order is **MLA pesarattu**: the crepe with upma folded inside. The name is usually traced to the canteen of the MLA quarters in Hyderabad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The breakfast that marks a Telugu kitchen, and today's offline task.
spotlights.memory_hook: Green gram, no ferment, upma inside.

spotlights.name: Ulavacharu

where.label: Krishna and Guntur districts, linked with Vijayawada

spotlights.spot_it: A thick, dark brown soup, glossy and tangy, often finished with a spoon of cream.
spotlights.story_md: Ulavalu is horse gram, a hardy legume grown in dry country and long thought of as animal fodder. Boiled for hours, then strained, its water is cooked down with tamarind, jaggery and spices into ulavacharu, a dark, thick, sour-sweet soup. Because it takes so long, it was a village dish made in big pots. Vijayawada restaurants turned it into a signature, served with rice and a spoon of fresh cream on top, and packaged ulavacharu is now sold across the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A poor man's legume turned into a city's signature dish.
spotlights.memory_hook: Horse gram, hours of boiling, cream on top.

spotlights.name: Ragi sangati with natu kodi
spotlights.when: Daily food of the dry interior
spotlights.spot_it: Smooth brown balls of finger millet next to a thin, fiery country-chicken curry.
spotlights.story_md: In Rayalaseema, where rain is scarce and rice was once a luxury, the staple is **ragi sangati**: finger-millet flour stirred into boiling water (often with a little rice) until it becomes a heavy dough, then shaped into balls. You do not chew it: you pinch off a piece, dip it in curry and swallow. The classic pairing is **natu kodi pulusu**, a thin, very hot curry of free-range country chicken. Farmers say it keeps you full through a day in the fields. Neighbouring Karnataka calls the same ball ragi mudde.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The food of the dry country, the counterweight to the delta's rice.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pinch, dip, swallow: do not chew the sangati.

spotlights.name: Godavari pulasa

where.label: Godavari near Rajahmundry, Yanam and Konaseema

spotlights.spot_it: A silver, bony river fish cooked in a tamarind pulusu in a clay pot, sold at startling prices.
spotlights.story_md: Pulasa is the Godavari name for the hilsa, the fish Bengal calls ilish. It lives in the sea and swims up the river to spawn when the monsoon floods turn the water red. Fishermen say the fresh red water changes its taste, and a fish caught in the Godavari during the floods (pulasa) is prized far above the same species caught at sea (vilasa). Prices run to thousands of rupees a kilo. It is cooked as a slow tamarind pulusu in a clay pot and eaten the next day. A Godavari saying: sell even your mangalsutra, but eat pulasa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A seasonal luxury that ties delta life to the river's floods.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sell your mangalsutra, eat pulasa.

spotlights.name: Guntur chilli
spotlights.spot_it: Mountains of red dried chillies in a market yard, with sneezing buyers.
spotlights.story_md: Andhra food is hot, and the heat has a supply chain. Guntur's Mirchi Yard is described as the largest chilli market in Asia. Each harvest season, trucks unload sacks of dried red chillies, and traders from China, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and the Gulf bid for varieties such as Guntur Sannam and Teja. The state grows somewhere between a quarter and two-fifths of India's chillies, depending on the year and the source. Walk through the yard and your eyes water and you will sneeze: that is part of the visit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Explains why the food burns: the chilli is local.
spotlights.memory_hook: Guntur: the yard where you cannot stop sneezing.

sections.title: Sweets and drinks
sections.intro_md:
Telugu sweets are about place: each famous one is tied to a town, and four of them have legal protection. The Tirupati laddu (GI 2009), Bandar laddu from Machilipatnam (GI 2017) and Atreyapuram pootharekulu (GI 2023) are protected names; Kakinada and Tapeswaram fight over the kaja. Ariselu, discs of rice flour and jaggery, are the Sankranti sweet.

Drinks follow the day. Morning is filter coffee in towns. Summer is majjiga, thin buttermilk with ginger, green chilli and curry leaves. At Sri Rama Navami there is panakam, jaggery water with pepper and cardamom. In the villages, from the palms, there is kallu, toddy, sweet at dawn and sour by dusk. And in the Araku hills the state grows its own coffee.

spotlights.name: Pootharekulu
spotlights.spot_it: Paper-thin, translucent sheets folded into rolls with sugar or jaggery and ghee.
spotlights.story_md: Pootharekulu means 'coated sheets'. A thin batter of rice starch is spread on the outside of a hot, upturned clay pot. In seconds it sets into a sheet as thin as tissue paper, and the maker, usually a woman working with three fingers and a wet cloth, peels it off. Others layer the sheets with powdered sugar or jaggery and ghee, sometimes dry fruit, and fold them into packets. Atreyapuram village makes them in thousands. The sweet-makers' association that holds the GI tag carries the name of Arthur Cotton, whose dam watered the delta.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A sweet that looks impossible, and a village that lives by it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sweet made on the outside of an upside-down pot.

spotlights.name: Tirupati laddu
spotlights.spot_it: A fist-sized golden laddu studded with cashews and raisins, handed out after darshan.
spotlights.story_md: The laddu given at Tirumala is a temple offering (prasadam) made by the temple trust in its kitchen, the Laddu Potu, by hundreds of cooks. Records date it to 1715. Gram flour, sugar, ghee, cashews, raisins and cardamom go in, in quantities measured in tonnes each day. It got a GI tag in 2009, so no one else can sell a 'Tirupati laddu'. In September 2024 the Chief Minister alleged animal fat in the ghee. A CBI-led investigation reported in January 2026 that fake ghee from vegetable oils had been supplied, and found no animal fat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A sweet that is also a legal brand and, since 2024, a court file.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only laddu with a GI tag and a chargesheet.

spotlights.name: Kakinada kaja
spotlights.spot_it: A fried, tube-like pastry that bursts with sugar syrup when bitten.
spotlights.story_md: Kaja is a fried pastry of layered wheat dough soaked in sugar syrup. The Kakinada version, also called gottam kaja (tube kaja) or Kotayya kaja after the sweet shop that made it famous, is rolled into a tube so the syrup stays inside: crisp outside, wet inside, and it squirts when you bite. Its neighbour, the Tapeswaram kaja, is the opposite: dry, flaky and layered like a croissant. Coastal Andhra argues about which is better the way other places argue about football.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two towns, two kajas, one long argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kakinada squirts; Tapeswaram flakes.

spotlights.name: Bandar laddu
spotlights.spot_it: A soft, crumbly gram-flour laddu with a strong taste of jaggery and ghee.
spotlights.story_md: Bandar is the old name of Machilipatnam, the port town; it simply means port. Its laddu, also called tokkudu laddu ('pounded laddu'), is made by frying gram flour into small drops, then pounding them with jaggery and ghee in a mortar until they bind. That pounding gives a dense, soft, crumbly texture, unlike the firm laddus of north India. Sweet makers in the town trace the recipe to Bundelkhand migrants in the 19th century. It became a GI product on 3 May 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The port town's sweet, protected by law.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bandar means port; tokkudu means pounded.

spotlights.name: Filter coffee and Araku coffee

where.label: Towns statewide; coffee grown in the Araku hills

spotlights.spot_it: Frothy milky coffee poured between a steel tumbler and a steel bowl to cool it.
spotlights.story_md: In Andhra towns the morning starts with filter coffee: dark decoction dripped slowly through a two-part steel filter, mixed with hot milk and sugar, then poured from height between a tumbler and a small bowl (dabara) until it foams. The state also grows coffee. In the Araku hills Adivasi farmers grow Arabica under shade trees, organically, often on small plots organised through cooperatives. For decades it sold as an anonymous commodity. In 2017 a brand built around it opened a café in Paris, and Araku coffee now sells as a premium single-origin bean.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A daily habit, and an Adivasi crop that went to Paris.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pour it high, foam it up; the beans come from Araku.

spotlights.name: Kallu, palm toddy
spotlights.when: Tapped year-round; sweetest in the morning
spotlights.spot_it: Milky white sap poured from a clay pot, drunk from a leaf cup or cupped hands under the palms.
spotlights.story_md: Kallu is the sap of palmyra (thati) and date palms. A tapper climbs the trunk with a loop of rope, cuts the flower stalk and ties a pot under it. Collected at dawn and drunk at once, the sap is sweet and barely alcoholic; that fresh form, neera, is sold as a health drink. By evening wild yeasts have turned it sour and mildly intoxicating. In villages kallu is drunk at roadside sheds, often with spicy fried snacks, and tapping is the hereditary work of particular castes. It is legal under licence and taxed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The oldest drink in the countryside, and a living caste occupation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sweet at dawn, sour by dusk.

sections.title: Festivals
sections.intro_md:
The Telugu year has one giant and many middle-sized festivals.

**Sankranti** in mid-January is the giant, above all on the coast: the one week when city Telugus go home. It runs four days: Bhogi with its bonfires, Sankranti with new clothes and muggulu, Kanuma for the cattle, Mukkanuma to close. Haridasus sing at dawn, gangireddu bulls bow at the door, kites fill the sky, and in the Godavari districts the cockfights run.

**Ugadi** (March or April) is the Telugu New Year. Then Sri Rama Navami, Vinayaka Chaturthi, the nine-day Brahmotsavam at Tirumala, Dasara at Vijayawada's Kanaka Durga temple, Atla Taddi for women, Deepavali, Christmas, Eid and Muharram's Rottela Panduga at Nellore. And once every twelve years, the Godavari Pushkaralu: next in 2027.

data.name: Rottela Panduga moves with Muharram (lunar calendar)

spotlights.name: Muggulu
spotlights.when: Daily at dawn; month-long contests before Sankranti
spotlights.spot_it: White rice-flour patterns on a swept, wetted doorstep, sometimes filled with colour.
spotlights.story_md: Before sunrise women sweep the ground in front of the house, sprinkle it with water (once, cow-dung water), and draw a muggu with rice flour pinched between the fingers. The simplest are lines around a grid of dots (chukkala muggu). In the month before Sankranti they grow until they fill the street, with colours, flowers and greetings, and colonies hold contests. On top sit gobbemmalu, small balls of cow dung topped with pumpkin flowers. The rice flour also feeds ants and birds: the pattern is meant to be eaten.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how art is part of a Telugu morning, not a museum.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice-flour art you leave for the ants.

spotlights.name: Haridasu

where.label: Villages and towns, during the Sankranti month

spotlights.spot_it: A man in saffron with a copper pot on his head, cymbals in hand, singing at your door at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: Through the month before Sankranti, a Haridasu walks the streets at dawn singing the names of Vishnu, 'Harilo ranga hari', with chidatalu (small cymbals) and sometimes a tambura. On his head he balances a copper vessel, the akshaya patra, decorated with flowers. He does not stop or speak much; families pour rice into the vessel, and it is considered lucky. The vessel stays balanced all morning. Children dress up as Haridasus for school festivals. The tradition is fading in cities but returns every January.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sound that tells a Telugu household Sankranti is coming.
spotlights.memory_hook: A copper pot that never falls, and rice for the singer.

spotlights.name: Gangireddulu

where.label: House to house, coastal villages and towns

spotlights.spot_it: A bull draped in patchwork cloths and bells, nodding yes at the door to a pipe and drum.
spotlights.story_md: At Sankranti, families of handlers (gangireddula vallu) walk decorated bulls from house to house. The bull wears layered, bright patchwork cloths, a tall headdress, bells and painted horns. A handler plays the sannayi (a nadaswaram-type reed pipe) and a drum, and the bull performs: it nods 'yes' to questions, kneels, bows to the householder, and lifts a hoof to bless. The family gives grain, clothes or money. It is a farmers' festival honouring cattle, and on Kanuma, the day after Sankranti, every family's own cattle are washed, painted and garlanded too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cattle at the centre of a harvest festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bull that bows and nods yes.

spotlights.name: Kodi pandalu, the Sankranti cockfights

where.label: Godavari and Krishna districts, Bhimavaram above all

spotlights.spot_it: A dirt ring under festival tents, crowds in white shirts, two roosters with blades on their legs.
spotlights.story_md: Every January, in villages of the Godavari delta, organisers clear fields, put up tents, lights and food stalls, and stage cockfights. Small curved blades are tied to the roosters' legs, and a fight can end in seconds. Owners raise fighting breeds for months on special diets. The fights are illegal: the Hyderabad High Court banned them in 2014 and the Supreme Court upheld the ban. They happen anyway at hundreds of sites, with bets the press estimates in the hundreds of crores of rupees, and local politicians in the front row.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clearest case of custom beating law in the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Banned since 2014; staged every January anyway.

spotlights.name: Bhogi fires and Sankranti kites
spotlights.when: Bhogi is the first day of Sankranti, mid-January
spotlights.spot_it: Bonfires in the street before dawn, and later, a sky full of kites.
spotlights.story_md: Sankranti runs four days. It opens with **Bhogi**: before dawn, families pile old wood, broken furniture and things they no longer need on a street bonfire, the Bhogi manta, and stand around it in the cold. The idea is to burn the old year. That evening small children are showered with bhogi pallu, a mix of jujube fruit, flower petals and coins, to ward off evil. Through the festival, kites fly from terraces, especially in towns, and children compete to cut each other's strings. Then come Sankranti, Kanuma for the cattle, and Mukkanuma.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The fire and the sky of the state's biggest festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burn the old at dawn, cut a kite string by noon.

spotlights.name: Ugadi pachadi
spotlights.when: Ugadi, Telugu New Year, March or April
spotlights.spot_it: A small bowl of thin chutney with neem flowers, mango bits and jaggery: bitter, sweet and sour in one spoon.
spotlights.story_md: On Ugadi, the Telugu New Year, everyone eats a spoonful of ugadi pachadi before anything else. It mixes six tastes: neem flowers for bitter, jaggery for sweet, tamarind for sour, raw mango for tang, salt, and chilli or pepper for heat. The point is that the coming year will bring all six, and you should accept them together. In the evening a priest reads the panchanga sravanam, the year's forecast, and politicians attend to hear their horoscopes read out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole philosophy of the year in one spoon.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six tastes, one spoon, one year.

spotlights.name: Godavari Pushkaralu

where.label: Rajahmundry and ghats along the Godavari

spotlights.spot_it: Millions of pilgrims packed on river steps, bathing at dawn for twelve days.
spotlights.story_md: Each of India's twelve sacred rivers has its Pushkaram once every twelve years, when Jupiter enters its zodiac sign; for the Godavari that is Leo (Simha). For twelve days pilgrims bathe, offer rites for their ancestors and listen to discourses, and Rajahmundry becomes one of the largest gatherings on earth. The cost of crowds is real: on the opening day of the 2015 Pushkaralu, 14 July, a crush at Rajahmundry's Pushkar ghat killed at least 27 people. The next Godavari Pushkaralu is in 2027; the state expects up to 10 crore visitors and has been building new ghats.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's largest event of 2027, and a test of crowd management.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every 12 years, when Jupiter enters Leo, the Godavari fills with people.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Start with what the data warns. The People of India project recorded roughly 386 to 390 communities in undivided Andhra Pradesh, among the most of any state, so any sentence that begins 'Andhra people are' averages over all of them. What sociologists do find is structure. Political power has sat with landowning castes that are not large: Kammas (about 5%) and Reddys (about 6 to 8%, by press estimates), with Kapus pushing for a Chief Minister of their own. Marriage to a cross-cousin or maternal uncle is allowed and common: NFHS-5 puts marriage between relatives at 18 to 28% in the southern states, against 11% nationally. Andhra has India's highest female sterilisation rate, 69.6%.

Three habits recur: education as a ladder (Narayana and Sri Chaitanya coaching began here), cinema fused with politics, and a taste for satire. The spotlights show what you would notice on a visit: how people eat, dress and marry.

spotlights.name: Eating on a banana leaf, with the right hand
spotlights.spot_it: Guests in a row, each with a leaf, mixing rice and curry with the fingers of the right hand.
spotlights.story_md: At weddings, festivals and many restaurants, meals are served on a banana leaf. The leaf is laid with its tip to the eater's left and sprinkled with water. You eat with your right hand only: the left is for passing dishes and is never put in the food. Rice is mixed with each curry by hand, a little at a time, and lifted with the fingertips, which many people say is part of the taste. When you are done, folding the leaf towards you means you were satisfied; at a funeral meal it is folded the other way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Table manners that tell an outsider at once what is polite.
spotlights.memory_hook: Right hand only; fold the leaf towards you.

spotlights.name: Langa voni, the half-sari

where.label: Statewide, Telugu and other south Indian homes

spotlights.when: From puberty to marriage, now festivals
spotlights.spot_it: A long flared skirt, a blouse, and a half-length sari cloth draped across the chest.
spotlights.story_md: Langa voni is the dress of the in-between years: a girl wears it from puberty until marriage, when she moves to the full sari. It has three pieces: the langa, a long skirt tied at the waist; a blouse; and the voni (or oni), a cloth of about 2 to 2.5 metres draped diagonally across the body and over one shoulder. Many families hold a langa voni ceremony when a girl first wears one, with relatives and gifts. Today most girls wear it only at festivals and weddings, but on Sankranti and Ugadi streets fill with silk half-saris.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dress that marks an age, not just an occasion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Langa, blouse, voni: the dress between girlhood and marriage.

spotlights.name: Telugu wedding: jeelakarra bellam
spotlights.spot_it: Bride and groom, a cloth screen just lowered between them, each with a hand on the other's head.
spotlights.story_md: The legal and ritual centre of a Hindu Telugu wedding is not the tying of the thread but **jeelakarra bellam**. Bride and groom sit facing each other with a cloth screen between them so they cannot see each other. At the exact muhurtham chosen by the priest, the screen drops, and each places a paste of cumin (jeelakarra) and jaggery (bellam) on the crown of the other's head. Cumin is bitter, jaggery sweet: the couple promises to share both. Then come the mangalsutra and talambralu, where the couple shower each other with rice coloured with turmeric.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Telugu way of saying 'for better or worse'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bitter cumin, sweet jaggery, on each other's heads.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Many of the state's people appear in the spotlights above: Nagarjuna, Annamacharya, Vemana, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Pingali Venkayya, Potti Sriramulu. A few more to know by name:

- **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** (1848 to 1919), Rajahmundry reformer: arranged the first Telugu widow remarriage in 1881.
- **Gurajada Apparao** (1862 to 1915): his play *Kanyasulkam* (1892) began modern Telugu drama.
- **Tanguturi Prakasam** (1872 to 1957), Andhra Kesari: first Chief Minister of Andhra State.
- **Jiddu Krishnamurti** (1895 to 1986), born in Madanapalle.
- **Neelam Sanjiva Reddy** (1913 to 1996): first CM of Andhra Pradesh, later President of India.
- **S. P. Balasubrahmanyam** (1946 to 2020), playback singer from Nellore district.
- **Karnam Malleswari** (born 1975), weightlifter: first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal, Sydney 2000.

spotlights.name: N. T. Rama Rao
spotlights.spot_it: A film star in a crown, blue-painted as Krishna or Rama; later, a politician in saffron.
spotlights.story_md: NTR acted in about 300 films and played Krishna and Rama so often that fans worshipped him as a god on screen. In 1982 he founded the Telugu Desam Party, campaigned across the state in a converted van he called the Chaitanya Ratham, appealed to 'Telugu self-respect' against the Congress in Delhi, and became Chief Minister within nine months, in January 1983. He served three times. His son-in-law N. Chandrababu Naidu took the party from him in 1995 and is Chief Minister today. NTR set the pattern of stars in Telugu politics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founder of the party that runs the state now, and of film-star politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Played the gods, then ran the state.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
If you went, how would you string the spotlights together? Four loops.

**North**: Visakhapatnam's beach road and Simhachalam, then the slow train to Araku, stopping at the Borra caves. **Godavari**: Rajahmundry, a boat through the Papikondalu, Konaseema's coconut delta, pootharekulu at Atreyapuram, kaja at Kakinada, and in January the cockfights. **Krishna and Guntur**: the Amaravati stupa and the new capital, Undavalli's four-storey rock-cut caves, Kuchipudi village, Kondapalli, Mangalagiri, and chillies at Guntur. **South and Rayalaseema**: Tirumala and Srikalahasti, flamingos at Pulicat with Sriharikota beyond, then west to Gandikota, the Belum caves and Lepakshi's hanging pillar.

sections.title: Ten things you did not know
sections.intro_md:
1. Andhra Pradesh farms about 70% of India's shrimp; from space its coast looks like graph paper.
2. India's rockets launch from Sriharikota, an island between a flamingo lagoon and the sea.
3. A piece of Puducherry, Yanam, sits inside the Godavari delta.
4. The coastline grew 79 km in 2025 because it was measured again on a better map.
5. Andhra State (1953) came out of a man's fast to death.
6. The capital was named in law only in April 2026, backdated to 2 June 2024.
7. The flag that became the tricolour was first sketched by a man from near Machilipatnam.
8. The English East India Company's first east-coast trading post was at Machilipatnam, in 1611.
9. One pillar at Lepakshi does not quite touch the floor.
10. Simhachalam's god is hidden under sandalwood paste for all but one day a year.

sections.title: How the state earns
sections.intro_md:
The economy was about ₹17.6 lakh crore in 2025-26, around eighth among states; the 2026-27 budget assumes ₹19.75 lakh crore. Income per person is about ₹2.98 lakh, richer than India's average, poorer than its southern neighbours.

The shape is unusual. Agriculture and allied activities make up about **37%**, against under a fifth for India, because fish, shrimp, livestock and fruit count as agriculture and are big money here. The state produced about 30% of India's fish in 2022-23. Rice grows in the deltas; chilli and tobacco around Guntur; groundnut in Rayalaseema; coffee in the Araku hills.

Industry clusters on the coast: Visakhapatnam's port, steel plant, shipyard and pharma; Krishnapatnam and Kakinada ports; Sri City on the Tamil Nadu border; a Kia plant in Anantapur. The weak point is debt: outstanding liabilities are about 36% of GSDP in 2026-27.

spotlights.name: Shrimp and fish ponds
spotlights.spot_it: Rectangular ponds to the horizon, each with a paddle-wheel aerator churning the water.
spotlights.story_md: Fly over the deltas and the land looks like graph paper: thousands of rectangular ponds where rice fields used to be. Andhra Pradesh grows about 70% of India's farmed shrimp, mostly Pacific white shrimp, and about 30% of its fish. Paddle-wheel aerators run day and night to keep oxygen up. The money is large and so are the side effects: salt water seeps into fields and drinking water, ponds eat into Kolleru Lake, and prices swing with foreign demand. When the United States raised tariffs on Indian goods in 2025, the Chief Minister asked the Centre to seek an exemption for shrimp.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest change to the delta landscape in a generation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Graph paper from the sky: 70% of India's farmed shrimp.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
*Checked on 25 October 2026.*

Since 12 June 2024 the state has been run by the TDP, Jana Sena and BJP alliance, which won 164 of 175 seats. Chief Minister **N. Chandrababu Naidu** is in his fourth term; Deputy Chief Minister **Pawan Kalyan** is a film star. The YSR Congress of **Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy** fell to 11 seats. The TDP's 16 MPs help keep the Modi government in office, which gives the state pull in Delhi. The next Assembly election is due in 2029.

The big stories: Amaravati and Polavaram (below); a Google AI data-centre hub at Visakhapatnam (about US$15 billion, ground broken 28 April 2026); an AM/NS steel plant at Anakapalli; the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant's survival; a Godavari-to-Rayalaseema water link disputed by Telangana; Cyclone Montha (28 October 2025); and the laddu case. Coming up: Godavari Pushkaralu and the census (2027), Amaravati's main buildings (2028), elections (2029).

spotlights.name: Amaravati, the new capital

where.label: South bank of the Krishna between Vijayawada and Guntur

spotlights.spot_it: Wide new roads through paddy fields, cranes, and half-built towers.
spotlights.story_md: When Telangana took Hyderabad in 2014, Andhra Pradesh had no capital. Farmers pooled about 33,000 acres near the old Satavahana capital, and the Prime Minister laid a foundation stone on 22 October 2015. Then politics stopped it: from 2019 the next government pushed three capitals instead, and work froze. Relaunched on 2 May 2025, the project had about ₹51,000 crore of works awarded by June 2026. On 1 and 2 April 2026 Parliament amended the 2014 Act to say 'Amaravati shall be the new capital', so only Parliament can now undo it. Major buildings are due in 2028.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's biggest bet, and the reason its debt matters.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital named after a Buddhist stupa, written into law in 2026.

spotlights.name: Polavaram dam
spotlights.spot_it: A long concrete spillway with dozens of gates across the Godavari where it leaves the hills.
spotlights.story_md: Polavaram is a multipurpose dam on the Godavari, made a national project in 2014 so the Centre pays for its irrigation part. It is meant to irrigate the delta and the uplands, send water to the Krishna, and one day south to Rayalaseema. A review on 12 October 2026 put physical progress at 90.1%, with the spillway, the main dam and the cofferdams done. The weak part is people: rehabilitation of displaced families, most of them Adivasi, stood at 51.9%. Its reservoir will flood villages upstream and part of the Papikondalu gorge.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's water future and its largest displacement.
spotlights.memory_hook: 90% concrete, 52% resettled.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
1. A coastal state of deltas, hills and lagoons, and a dry interior, Rayalaseema, joined by a 1937 promise about water that still drives its politics.
2. Two thousand years ago the lower Krishna was a Buddhist heartland; Amaravati's sculpture now sits in London, Chennai and Paris.
3. Andhra State (1953) came out of a 58-day fast; Andhra Pradesh (1956) took in Telangana; Telangana left in 2014.
4. Things to recognise on sight: Kuchipudi's brass plate, pen versus block Kalamkari, Kondapalli wood and Etikoppaka lac, gongura, pootharekulu, a gangireddu bull, a Haridasu's copper pot.
5. Now: Amaravati is the legal capital since April 2026, Polavaram is 90% built but half its displaced families wait, and debt sits at 36% of GSDP.

cards.front: Which classical dance is this, and what is she holding?
cards.back: Kuchipudi, in the tarangam: the dancer keeps time on the rim of a brass plate.

cards.front: Which of these two is Kuchipudi?
cards.back: The left (brass plate, rounded movement). The right is Bharatanatyam: angular, deep half-sitting stance.

cards.front: Name this puppet tradition and the material the puppets are made of.
cards.back: Tholu bommalata. Thin, painted, translucent leather (goat or deer hide).

cards.front: Three performers, one with a tambura in the middle. Name the form.
cards.back: Burra katha: a lead singer with tambura and two side players with drums who joke and comment.

cards.front: What is special about how this veena is made, and where?
cards.back: Bobbili veena: carved from a single block of jackfruit wood, near Bobbili, Vizianagaram. GI tag 2011.

cards.front: Pen or block? Which Kalamkari is from Srikalahasti?
cards.back: The left: freehand pen, story panels of gods. The right is Machilipatnam: block-printed, repeating floral motifs.

cards.front: Name these toys and the wood they are carved from.
cards.back: Kondapalli toys, carved from light tella poniki wood and joined with makku (tamarind seed paste).

cards.back: The right: Etikoppaka, shiny and rounded, coloured with lac. The left: Kondapalli, carved and painted.

cards.back: Lac with plant dyes is pressed onto the spinning wood; friction heat melts it into a hard skin. No paint.

cards.front: Which temple has this pillar, and what is odd about it?
cards.back: Veerabhadra temple, Lepakshi (about 1530). Its base does not quite touch the floor.

cards.front: Where is this giant stone bull?
cards.back: Lepakshi, Sri Sathya Sai district: a Nandi carved from one granite boulder.

cards.front: Which school of sculpture made this panel, and roughly when?
cards.back: The Amaravati school, 2nd century CE. It shows the Buddha's Great Departure. Now in the Guimet Museum, Paris.

cards.front: Name the temple under this gold tower.
cards.back: Venkateswara temple, Tirumala, above Tirupati.

cards.front: What covers the image of the god at Simhachalam, and when is it removed?
cards.back: Sandalwood paste, all year. It is removed only on Akshaya Tritiya (Chandanotsavam).

cards.front: Srikalahasti's name joins three devotees. Who?
cards.back: Sri the spider, Kala the snake, Hasti the elephant. Shiva is worshipped there as wind (Vayu).

cards.front: A priest on the tip of a long pole over a crowd. Which festival?
cards.back: Sirimanu utsavam of Pydithalli Ammavaru, Vizianagaram: a village-goddess jatara.

cards.front: These flamingos feed in a lagoon whose sand bar holds what?
cards.back: Pulicat Lake. Its barrier island, Sriharikota, is ISRO's launch site.

cards.front: Name this gorge and its river.
cards.back: Gandikota, on the Penna, Kadapa district. Sold as India's Grand Canyon.

cards.front: Which river runs through these hills, and what will change the view?
cards.back: The Godavari through the Papikondalu. The Polavaram reservoir will drown part of the gorge.

cards.front: Name this dance and the hills it belongs to.
cards.back: Dhimsa, danced by Adivasi women in the Araku hills (and Koraput in Odisha).

cards.front: This pelican nests at which lake between the two deltas?
cards.back: Kolleru, between the Godavari and Krishna deltas. Ramsar site since 2002.

cards.front: Name this relish and the leaf it is made from.
cards.back: Gongura pachadi, from roselle leaves: sour and hot, eaten with raw onion.

cards.front: What is in this jar, and what is left inside each piece?
cards.back: Avakaya: raw mango with mustard, chilli and oil. The hard stone stays in.

cards.front: Name this breakfast and its main grain.
cards.back: Pesarattu, made of whole green gram. With upma inside it is 'MLA pesarattu'.

cards.front: Name these brown balls and the region they come from.
cards.back: Ragi sangati (finger millet), Rayalaseema. Eaten with natu kodi (country chicken) curry.

cards.front: What is pulasa, and when is it caught?
cards.back: Hilsa caught in the Godavari during the monsoon floods (July to September). Prized and very expensive.

cards.front: What is ulavacharu made from?
cards.back: Horse gram (ulavalu), boiled for hours; a thick, sour-sweet soup linked with Vijayawada.

cards.front: Which town has Asia's largest chilli market yard?
cards.back: Guntur. Andhra grows roughly a quarter to two-fifths of India's chillies.

cards.back: Pootharekulu, Atreyapuram. Sheets are set on the outside of a hot upturned pot. GI tag 2023.

cards.front: Which laddu has a GI tag (2009) and a 2026 chargesheet?
cards.back: The Tirupati laddu, made in the temple's Laddu Potu kitchen.

cards.back: Port. Bandar is the old name of Machilipatnam. The laddu is pounded (tokkudu). GI 2017.

cards.back: Kallu, palm toddy: sweet and barely alcoholic at dawn (neera), sour and intoxicating by evening.

cards.back: Muggulu, drawn at dawn before the house. Rice flour also feeds ants and birds.

cards.back: A Haridasu, in the month before Sankranti, singing Vishnu's names and collecting rice.

cards.back: A gangireddu: it nods yes, kneels and bows to a pipe and drum at Sankranti.

cards.back: Custom, big betting money and political patronage: local leaders attend and organisers set up rings at hundreds of sites.

cards.front: How often is the Godavari Pushkaralu held, and when next?
cards.back: Once every 12 years, when Jupiter enters Leo. Next in 2027, centred on Rajahmundry.

cards.front: What are they placing on each other's heads?
cards.back: Jeelakarra bellam: a paste of cumin and jaggery, bitter and sweet, at the exact wedding muhurtham.

cards.front: Name this dress and who traditionally wears it.
cards.back: Langa voni (half-sari): skirt, blouse and voni, worn by girls from puberty until marriage.

cards.back: The right hand only. Folding it towards you means you are satisfied.

cards.front: Who designed this 1921 flag, and what did Gandhi add?
cards.back: Pingali Venkayya (red and green). Gandhi asked for the white stripe and the spinning wheel.

cards.front: How long did Potti Sriramulu fast, and what did it lead to?
cards.back: 58 days, ending with his death on 15 December 1952. Andhra State formed 1 October 1953.

cards.front: What was the Rampa Rebellion?
cards.back: Adivasi uprising of 1922 to 1924 in the Godavari hills, led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, against forest laws banning podu.

cards.front: Which script is this, and why is it so round?
cards.back: Telugu. A common explanation: written on palm leaves with a stylus, where straight lines would split the leaf.

cards.front: This actor played gods on screen, then founded a party. Who and which party?
cards.back: N. T. Rama Rao, Telugu Desam Party, 1982. Chief Minister from January 1983.
